# Valuation model v2 — model card

**This is the current production artefact.** Generated by `ml/train_valuation.py`
(seeded, `RANDOM_STATE=42`). Re-run with `ml/.venv/bin/python ml/train_valuation.py`
to reproduce every number on this page (it also refreshes `ml/artifacts/valuation-v1/`
for comparison). Uses the v3 postnummer->omrade mapping (task 4b, OSM tier 1 +
GeoNames tier 2 + same-prefix-neighbour tier 3 -- see `ml/mapping/README.md`).

## What price level a prediction represents (read this first)

**This model has no time feature.** A prediction is not "today's price" in the
sense of tracking a live market index -- it is the **average price level observed
across the training period, 2026-01-01 to 2026-08-31 (8 months)**. There is no
month/date input anywhere in the RESTRICTED feature set the product uses (see
"Inputs available at inference" in `ml/artifacts/valuation-v1/MODEL_CARD.md` and
"'Today' / time reference" below), so the model cannot and does not distinguish a
January 2026 transaction from an August 2026 one -- it was trained on the pooled
8-month period and predicts that pooled average level for any input, regardless of
when the prediction is requested.

**Drift check** (done once, on the FULL feature set which *did* include a
`month_num` term, specifically to check whether dropping time was safe): an OLS
regression of log(price_per_sqm) on `month_num` (1-8) among the other features
found **+0.32% per calendar month, 95% CI [-0.01%, +0.65%], p=0.054** -- not
statistically significant at the conventional 5% level. In other words: **no
statistically detectable price trend across Jan-Aug 2026** in this data. This is
the empirical justification for treating "the Jan-Aug 2026 average" as a reasonable
stand-in for "today" -- if the market had shown a clear trend, dropping the time
feature would have been a real approximation error, not just a missing-input
convenience.

**What this means for the product**: "today" in the product's price check
effectively means **"the Jan-Aug 2026 price level"** until this model is retrained
on more recent data. If Binfo's transaction data continues to accumulate and a
future retrain shows a detectable trend (the current p=0.054 is close enough to
0.05 that more data could easily flip this either way), predictions will need a
time feature reinstated (see "'Today' / time reference" below) and this
"average-of-the-period" approximation will need to be revisited -- flagged
explicitly as a assumption with a real (if currently small and statistically
unconfirmed) expiry risk, not a permanent design decision.

## What changed since the last update (mapping v2 -> v3, second follow-up)

1. **Mapping fix, round 2**: training-row area coverage rose from 92.5% to
   **99.9%** (file 1: 4,967/4,973; file 2: 4,966/4,973 -- only 2 unique postcodes
   remain unmapped in total, both for documented, principled reasons, not gaps --
   see `ml/mapping/README.md`). This further improved model accuracy: FULL-feature
   LightGBM CV MAPE went from 12.42% to **12.23%**.
2. **Model-size experiment** (new, item 6): measured the MAPE cost of rounding
   leaf/threshold values to 6 significant digits and of capping the number of
   boosting rounds (trees) at 200 or 300 (of 400). All options cost well under the
   0.1-percentage-point bar set for this decision, so **the shipped model.json is
   now the compressed one**: 300 trees, 6-significant-figure rounding,
   **3,271,951 bytes (3.27 MB), down from 4,646,812 bytes (4.65 MB) uncompressed --
   a 29.6% reduction**, for a measured cost of **+0.0185 percentage points MAPE**
   (see "Model-size experiment" below for the full table and reasoning).
3. Everything else (restricted feature set, time+area-aware conformal interval,
   portable JSON export format, parity fixtures) is unchanged in method from the
   first v2 follow-up; only the numbers moved, because the underlying mapping and
   model changed.

## Model comparison (5-fold CV, MAPE on total price, v3 mapping)

| Model | FULL CV MAPE | RESTRICTED CV MAPE (shipped feature set) |
|---|---:|---:|
| Regularised log-linear (RidgeCV) | 16.15% | 16.16% |
| Random forest | 13.36% | 13.09% |
| **LightGBM** | **12.23%** | **12.24%** |
| XGBoost | 12.29% | 12.39% |

**Time-based split** (train Jan-Jun, test Jul-Aug):

| Model | FULL time-split MAPE | RESTRICTED time-split MAPE |
|---|---:|---:|
| Regularised log-linear (RidgeCV) | 17.37% | 16.89% |
| Random forest | 13.84% | 13.38% |
| **LightGBM** | 12.93% | **12.69%** |
| XGBoost | 12.91% | 12.58% |

LightGBM chosen for both FULL and RESTRICTED (same serving-simplicity reasoning as
before: see the "Model choice note" in the mapping-v2-era card, unchanged --
Random Forest's RESTRICTED CV MAPE, 13.09%, is within the 1pp margin but LightGBM
has the only standard, portable, cross-language JSON export). Restricted-vs-full
MAPE gap is **+0.01 percentage points** on CV -- again, no measurable cost from
dropping `building_storeys`/`month_num`.

The "Okänt" bucket is now tiny (24 rows, down from 392 before the mapping fix) --
essentially just rows with a missing/malformed postal_code in the raw data (18 of
them, per the cleaning report) plus the handful of genuinely-unmapped postcodes. Its
MAPE looks alarming (34.9%) but this is a very small, structurally-different
residual bucket (no area signal at all), not evidence the model got worse -- if
anything, this is the expected shape once almost everything else has a real area:
what's left really is the hardest 0.5% of rows. Small-n areas
(Centrala Stockholm n=12, Brannkyrka-Skarholmen n=50) remain noisy.

## Prediction intervals (time+area-aware split conformal)

Method unchanged from the previous update: train Jan-May, calibrate `q` per area
(log scale) on June (>=30 calibration rows, else pooled fallback), evaluate on
held-out Jul-Aug.

**Result: 88.3% empirical coverage overall** (n=888 test rows; target 90%). This is
essentially the same ballpark as the previous measurement (89.5%) -- the small
change reflects the different mapping (some rows moved between "Okänt" and a real
area, changing which area's June/Jul-Aug data backs each `q`), not a regression in
method.

**Per-area coverage** (held-out Jul-Aug test set):

| Area | n (test) | Coverage | q source |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Södermalm | 125 | 94.4% | area-specific |
| Östermalm | 107 | 92.5% | area-specific |
| Hägersten-Liljeholmen | 120 | 91.7% | area-specific |
| Hässelby-Vällingby | 32 | 87.5% | pooled fallback (n_calib<30) |
| Kungsholmen | 107 | 86.9% | area-specific |
| Vasastan-Norrmalm | 98 | 86.7% | area-specific |
| Bromma-Västerled | 85 | 85.9% | area-specific |
| Enskede-Skarpnäck | 92 | 85.9% | area-specific |
| Spånga-Kista | 28 | 82.1% | pooled fallback (n_calib<30) |
| Farsta-Vantör | 62 | 75.8% | area-specific |
| Brännkyrka-Skärholmen | 9 | 100.0% | pooled fallback (n_calib<30) |
| Essingen | 17 | 100.0% | pooled fallback (n_calib<30) |
| Centrala Stockholm | 1 | 100.0% | pooled fallback (n_calib<30) |
| Okänt (postnummer ej kartlagt) | 5 | 40.0% | pooled fallback (n_calib<30) |

Same caveats as before: Farsta-Vantör remains the one real, repeated miss (75.8%,
n=62, down slightly from 77.4% -- consistent, not noise from a single run). The
"Okänt" row (40.0%, n=5) is not meaningful at n=5 and should be ignored as a
coverage statistic -- it is reported for completeness, not as evidence of a
problem. The 100%-coverage rows are all very small test sets (n=1, 9, 17) and
likewise not strong evidence of good calibration, just too few points to see a miss.

## Model-size experiment (task item 6)

Evaluated on the **independent time-split model** (trained Jan-Jun, tested on the
untouched Jul-Aug period) -- not the all-data production model, so this is an
honest, non-overfit measurement. A pure-Python tree evaluator was written and
sanity-checked against LightGBM's own native `predict()` (max absolute difference:
**0.00e+00**, i.e. exact) before being used to score the rounded/capped variants
(LightGBM's Python API has no "load a modified JSON dump" method, so a custom, but
verified-identical, evaluator was necessary to test hypothetical modifications).

| Variant | MAPE | Δ vs baseline | JSON size | Size reduction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Baseline (400 trees, full precision) | 12.688% | — | 4,644,187 B | — |
| Rounded to 6 sig figs, 400 trees | 12.688% | +0.0001pp | 4,360,902 B | -6.1% |
| 300 trees, full precision | 12.707% | +0.0183pp | 3,482,640 B | -25.0% |
| **300 trees, rounded (SHIPPED)** | **12.707%** | **+0.0185pp** | **3,268,997 B** | **-29.6%** |
| 200 trees, full precision | 12.738% | +0.0497pp | 2,322,424 B | -50.0% |
| 200 trees, rounded | 12.738% | +0.0498pp | 2,178,795 B | -53.1% |

**Recommendation: 300 trees + 6-significant-figure rounding** (what is shipped).
Rounding alone is essentially free (+0.0001pp, since 6 significant digits already
exceeds float32 precision for these value ranges) and worth doing regardless of tree
count. Tree-count capping is where the real size savings are, and the MAPE cost
scales roughly linearly with trees removed (200 trees costs ~2.7x what 300 trees
costs, consistent with removing roughly twice as many boosting rounds). 300 trees
was chosen over 200 as the shipped default because it keeps a larger safety margin
below the 0.1pp bar (0.0185pp used, vs 0.0498pp for 200) while still capturing most
of the available size reduction (30% vs 53%) -- diminishing returns from 200 trees
are much smaller in size (-53% vs -30%, +23 points) than the extra accuracy risk
taken on (+0.031pp extra, i.e. ~2.7x the accuracy cost for that extra 23 points of
compression). **200 trees + rounding remains a valid, still-under-the-0.1pp-bar
alternative** if server-side load time or storage becomes a tighter constraint later
-- both the 200-tree and 300-tree variants are well inside the brief's threshold,
this is a size/margin trade-off between two acceptable options, not a
safe-vs-unsafe one.

Per the brief's rule ("keep the shipped artefact the accuracy-first one unless the
loss is under 0.1 percentage points"): since the measured loss (0.0185pp) is
comfortably under that bar, **the shipped `model.json` is the compressed (300-tree,
rounded) version, not the full-precision 400-tree one.** `parity_fixtures.json` was
regenerated from the exact compressed model (via the same verified custom
evaluator), so it is consistent with what ships.

**Caveat**: the cost above was measured on the time-split model (trained on 6
months), not the exact all-data production model (trained on 8 months) that is
actually shipped -- there is no honest held-out set to measure the production
model's own compression cost on without leaking. We rely on the time-split
measurement as the best available evidence that the cost is negligible; there is no
specific reason to expect materially different sensitivity (same tree count, same
boosting algorithm, similar data distribution), but this is inference by analogy,
not a direct measurement of the exact shipped artefact.

## Serving artefact contents (unchanged structure from the previous update)

- **`model.json`**: `{feature_order_out, numeric_features, missing_indicator_features,
  categorical_features, numeric_medians_for_imputation,
  categorical_fill_value_for_imputation, categorical_onehot_categories,
  lightgbm_booster}`. `lightgbm_booster` is LightGBM's own `Booster.dump_model()`
  format, **truncated to the first 300 trees and with every `leaf_value`/`threshold`
  rounded to 6 significant digits** (see above) -- still valid, parseable
  LightGBM-dump-format JSON, just smaller.
- **Inference recipe**, **back-transform**, and **interval formula**: unchanged from
  the previous update -- see the "Serving artefact contents" section there, or
  `metadata.json` -> `production_model` in this artefact (kept in sync).
- **`parity_fixtures.json`**: 50 fixtures, regenerated against the compressed model
  (not the uncompressed one) so a TS evaluator implementing against `model.json`
  should reproduce these to floating-point precision.
- `model.joblib` **not** shipped (JSON is complete).

## "Today" / time reference

Unchanged: not used. See "What price level a prediction represents" at the top of
this card for the full statement (Jan-Aug 2026 pooled average, no detectable trend
found, p=0.054) and its product implication. Summary: the RESTRICTED feature set
has no time feature (the product supplies no valuation date at inference), and the
drift check found no statistically significant month-over-month trend in the
8-month training window, so treating the model's output as "today's" price is a
reasonable approximation for now -- but an approximation with a stated expiry
condition (see above), not a permanent guarantee.

## Effects table

Unchanged methodology (FULL feature set, unregularised OLS, interpretability only).
Numbers refreshed against the v3 mapping in `ml/artifacts/valuation-v1/coefficients.json`.

## Limitations (in addition to `ml/artifacts/valuation-v1/MODEL_CARD.md` and `ml/mapping/README.md`)

- Only **2 postcodes total** remain unmapped (1 training-file-1 postcode: 12364,
  prefix confirmed *not* Stockholm-only; 1 additional training-file-2 postcode:
  61071, confirmed outside the kommun entirely) -- both fall back to the "Okänt"
  category / Stockholm-wide model, correctly.
- Per-area conformal coverage still varies substantially (75.8%-100%), and
  Farsta-Vantör's under-coverage (75.8%, n=62) persists across both mapping
  versions -- this looks like a real, repeated pattern (not one-off noise) worth
  investigating further if interval precision in that specific area matters a lot.
- The 300-tree/6-sig-fig compression's accuracy cost was measured on a proxy model
  (time-split), not the exact shipped (all-data) model -- see caveat above.
- The model has no time-awareness -- it will not automatically reflect price
  changes after August 2026 without retraining.
- LightGBM/XGBoost were assumed unavailable per the original task brief but
  installed successfully in `ml/.venv` from PyPI. Random Forest remains the
  documented pure-scikit-learn fallback if that assumption is wrong for the real
  deployment environment (13.09% CV MAPE, RESTRICTED features -- 0.85pp worse than
  LightGBM, and would need a bespoke (unverified-format) JSON exporter to serve the
  same way).
